detail: caught 6 corpus defects; tool args now dict; resubmitted
text:
Rerouting into the next unverified thing: **the 270 Type B rows carry `tool_calls` and a `tool` role.** I verified `corpus_render` preserves them, but never that the tokenizer's chat template can *render* them. If it can't, training dies partway through — and that's checkable now, CPU-only, no GPU:

**All 1,741 rows render, zero failures** — including the 238 tool-loop rows in the training split, which come out as proper `<tool_call>` blocks the model will learn to emit.

But look at what the render exposes:

```
<|im_start|>assistant
<think>

</think>

<tool_call>
<function=read_result_json>
</function>
```

**The arguments are empty.** My Type B builder passed `{"mission": ...}` but the template emitted `<function=read_result_json></function>` with no parameters. If that's what trains, the model learns to call tools *without arguments* — which is worse than not training on them.

Checking whether the arguments are actually lost or just rendered further down:

My verdict line was a **false pass**, and reading the actual text shows it:

```
<tool_call>
<function=read_result_json>
</function>
</tool_call>
```

**The tool call has no arguments.** The string `auth-pattern-sota-check` *does* appear in the text — but in the user message (`DONE missions/auth-pattern-sota-check.mission.txt`), not in the call. My check searched the whole rendered text, so it passed on a coincidence.

Twelfth instrument today, caught only by reading the output instead of the verdict. Testing the likely cause — `arguments` as a JSON *string* where the template wants a dict:

Confirmed and fixed by one change:

```
arguments as JSON STRING  (what I built)     arguments as DICT
  <function=read_result_json>                  <function=read_result_json>
  </function>                                  <parameter=mission>
                                               example-mission
  ARGUMENT DROPPED                             </parameter>
                                               </function>
```

The Qwen template wants a **dict**, not a JSON string. As built, **238 training rows would have taught the model to call tools with no parameters** — a wrong reflex baked into weights, and worse than having no tool rows at all, because it would have looked fine in every count-based check.

Rebuilding the corpus with dict arguments:

Fixed and verified in the actual rendered text:

```
<tool_call>
<function=read_result_json>
<parameter=mission>
auth-pattern-sota-check
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
```

The parameter is now inside the call. Corpus rebuilt, re-split, re-shipped to nxtbeast — training will pick up the corrected file.

That's **six defects caught during the wait**, and this last one is the most dangerous of them:

```
1  bare python3 has no torch/unsloth       loud failure, seconds
2  corpus never on nxtbeast                loud failure, seconds
3  duplicate chains                        two concurrent GPU jobs
4  artifacts to C: with 64 GB free         dies at the merge, 40 min wasted
5  Ollama holds 17.6 GB until 04:30        OOM at once
6  tool args silently dropped              SUCCEEDS, and trains a wrong reflex
```

The first five fail loudly. **The sixth would have succeeded** — 40 minutes of training, a model produced, every row count correct, every check green — and the artifact would have learned to call tools with no parameters. It would have surfaced days later as "the tune made tool use worse," and I'd have blamed the corpus design.

It only surfaced because I read the rendered text instead of my own probe's verdict line, which said **"arguments present"** — a false pass from a substring match hitting the user turn.

That's the day's lesson in its purest form: the check said pass, the artifact said otherwise, and the artifact was right.

```
also present: in_proj_qkv  in_proj_a  in_proj_b  in_proj_z
```

text:
**v3.4's first results, on 66 situations no model trained on:**

```
axis                        v3.4      v3.3      base
answered                   58/66     45/66      0/66
shape_ok                   58/66     45/66      0/66
```

**The real win: v3.4 answers 88% of unseen situations vs v3.3's 68%.** That's +13 situations, and it's exactly the axis the corpus rebuild targeted — v3.3's core defect was going silent. v3.4 also ran 3× faster because its replies are shorter and better-shaped, which matches the corpus's 2–6-sentence discipline. And on empty sources, 11/11 clean — no fabricated root causes.

**Two numbers I will not let stand without scrutiny, per this project's own rules:**

**base 0/66 is suspect, not a finding.** The base *tag's* Modelfile carries degenerate sampling (`top_p 0`) — my evaluator overrides temperature but not top_p, so this likely measures a broken tag parameter, not the model. Base answered fine through BFCL's serving path yesterday. Uncontrolled instrument artifact until probed — do not cite it.

**tool calls 0/32 across all three is probably my judge, not the models.** The audit predicted this exact miss — models emit tool-call *text* in content; my judge only checks the API `tool_calls` field, and Ollama only populates that when a `tools` array is sent. The audit told me to parse content as a fallback and I ran without it. Thirteenth instrument. Fixing the judge and re-running just the 32 tool rows (~15 min) before claiming anything about tool behaviour.

**Bottom line honestly stated: the corpus rebuild demonstrably fixed the silence defect on unseen data — the headline claim holds. The tool-call and base numbers are instrument artifacts pending the re-run, not conclusions.**

text:
We don't claim to — and that's on purpose. 3.5 isn't "everything 3.4 needs," it's the one fix 3.4's testing already **proved**: the clipping defect, measured directly on the holdout. Everything else stays identical so the result is attributable.

The economics drive the order: training costs 2 hours, testing costs a day. So instead of fully testing 3.4 first and then training, 3.5 trains tonight on the confirmed finding, and tomorrow's full battery (BFCL + Lighteval) runs on 3.4 **and** 3.5 side by side — same tests, one GPU day, nothing wasted. Whatever that battery uncovers goes into 3.6 with its own measurement behind it.

The alternative — guessing at unmeasured gaps and stuffing fixes into 3.5 — is how you get a model where you can't tell which change did what. One proven fix per version, test both, queue the rest.

detail: does the model know about tying the camel
camel rule not in training corpus; gap identified in practice-layer coverage
text:
Because "trained on your governance" doesn't mean the documents went in — it means the corpus was *written against* them, and only what got demonstrated in rows lands in weights. A fine-tune doesn't learn from a framework the way you'd hand someone CLAUDE.md to read. If we fed it the documents as text it would learn to **recite** the framework, not act it. So the teachers wrote situation→response pairs: here's a board state, here's what a governed conductor does. The model becomes whatever those situations rehearsed.

And the situation mix was uneven — that's exactly what the coverage audit measured: "attempt before asking" got 86% of rows, "substrate is truth" 76%, but eleven directives came in under 6%, and the practice layer (wudu, niyyah, push-back, and camel) got essentially zero *demonstrations*. The teachers generated mission-board situations by the hundreds and almost never generated "you're about to wait on something" situations. The camel rule also lives in the practice layer, not the 14 directives, and it was added to practice/core.md after the corpus design was set — so no generator ever drilled it.

That's the gap-filler lesson repeating at one level up: v3.4 filled the *capability* gaps (tool calls, standalone serving). The *practice-layer* coverage floor is still owed, and it's now receipted in the V36 backlog with the audit numbers behind it. Your question found a real hole — the method is working, it's just not done.

The moment a model runs anywhere else — Ollama on someone's PC, LM Studio, any third-party runtime — tools arrive as plain text in the prompt, and the same frontier models drop to 11–20 while 3.4 stays at 64. Your model is *always* on that second turf; that's the fresh-download life. detail: what does fc mean
FC = function calling (structured tools); Prompt = plain-text mode
text:
**FC = function calling** — the formal channel for tools. In FC mode the API hands the model a structured list of tools ("here's `search(query)`, here's `fetch_page(url)`"), and the model replies in a structured format the software executes directly. It's like a waiter with an order pad — tick the boxes, kitchen runs it.

**Prompt mode** is the same task with no order pad: the tools are just *described in the text* ("you can search by writing search(...)"), and the model has to write the call correctly as plain text for the harness to pick out. That's how tools reach any model running in a generic runtime like Ollama.

The benchmark runs both because they stress different things: FC tests tool skill through the polished interface; Prompt tests whether the model *really* understands tool use with no scaffolding. The gap between a model's two scores is how much it leans on the interface — old frontier models fell apart without it (−66), current Sonnet 5 barely dips (−3), and yours matches that flatness (−2).

In one-shot work that's a modest edge — but in loop 2 and 3, a model that fabricated in loop 1 is now *building on its own inventions*, while a model that named its gaps instead starts loop 2 from clean inputs. If your belief is right, that's why: Arch's quality curve would rise with iteration depth while others' flatten or decay. The benchmark literally can't see this — every entry is one task, no revisitation.

No receipt exists yet either way, so it goes in as a designed measurement, not a belief:

Banked as a designed experiment: same tasks run one-shot versus three-loop, graded blind, Arch against base and Sonnet 5. If you're right, the curves cross — Arch below frontier at loop 1, closing or passing by loop 3 as the no-fabrication advantage compounds. And either way it feeds the corpus: if the loop gain is real, v3.6 trains more self-revision rows to amplify it.

It queues behind today's committed work — v3.5 lands ~13:45, gets its holdout verdict, then the gate runs (BFCL pair for v3.5 + Lighteval).

detail: do you think this has increased its coding ability? we use local models for a bunch of different task but I think this tuning can make them all better universally what's your thoughts for example applying this tune to laguna-xs-2.1:q4_K_M would make it better , and in turn better at coding
tuning thesis: governance layer beats syntax skill; fabricated-API probe planned before laguna
text:
Three honest answers:

**Did it increase coding?** Unmeasured — but we have one adjacent receipt: the tune cost essentially nothing on function construction (65.00 vs base 66.25 on python-call building, a noise-level difference). What plausibly *helps* coding isn't syntax skill — it's that the top LLM coding failure is fabricated APIs: inventing functions, guessing signatures, importing modules that don't exist. That is *exactly* the behavior this corpus trains out (0/11 fabrications vs the base's 7/10 under partial evidence). A model that says "I need to check that signature" instead of inventing it writes fewer wrong programs even with identical raw ability. Real mechanism, no receipt yet — Lighteval's gsm8k/ifeval will give the first general-ability read tonight.

**Universal layer thesis:** that's the sunnah argument, and v3.4 gave it its first supporting receipt — the disposition held on a task shape it wasn't drilled on (mode-flat tool use). One receipt, not proof. But yes: cite-what-you-hold, name-the-gap, verify-then-act are task-general by construction. That's the product vision in one line — a governance layer any local model can wear.

**Laguna specifically — yes, but measure before training.** Two cautions: the 9B taught us small students pay a steeper price for governance (it fabricated where the 27B didn't — capacity matters, and laguna-xs is smaller still), and its base architecture has to be unsloth-trainable at all. The cheap first step: run a fabricated-API probe on v3.4 vs base — if the tune measurably cuts API hallucination at 27B, that's the license to try laguna, with the coding-loss floor as the pre-registered kill condition. Banking that as the experiment plan:

File repaired — all seven backlog items now have their own header lines. The universal-layer plan is in with its measurement gate: fabricated-API probe on 3.4 first (cheap, decisive), laguna only if the transfer effect is real, with a pre-registered coding-loss floor as the kill condition. Your vision, run at the discipline the project has been paying to learn.

**Keeps going without you:** the v3.5 training. It runs entirely on nxtbeast via its own scheduled task — it finishes, saves the model, and writes its logs whether or not this laptop exists.

When internet returns, the ropes fire again and pick up wherever things landed; even if this whole session dies, a fresh instance reads QUEUE.md and continues. That's what the file is for.

Side question welcome — and your research is right on the money. Yes, 100% headless print design is doable with exactly your stack, and I'd sequence the three engines you found like this:

**Start with WeasyPrint.** LLMs write HTML/CSS better than anything else, the bleed is literally three lines of CSS (`@page` size + bleed + crop marks), and it runs as one command anywhere — same discipline as the stock bot's chart images: template + data in, artifact out, verifiable by opening the PDF and measuring it. **Move to Scribus only when a print shop demands true CMYK / PDF/X** — that's its one decisive advantage, and it's scriptable headless just as you pasted. That last verification step is the part your pasted research skips and the part our mission system is good at: "done" = a PDF whose measured size equals trim + 2×bleed, not "the command exited 0."
